questions.stem: A company sets up an internal CA, certificate templates, issuance and revocation policies, and automatic enrollment for its laptops. What BEST describes what it has built?

questions.stem: Cisco DMVPN is built from several technologies. Which two of these does it use? (Choose two.)

options.text: NHRP
options.rationale: Correct: spokes use it to find each other's addresses.

options.text: mGRE
options.rationale: Correct: multipoint GRE lets one interface reach many spokes.

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: An AAA protocol, not part of DMVPN.
Port access control, unrelated to DMVPN.

options.text: Static NAT
options.rationale: Not a DMVPN component.

questions.explanation: Cisco DMVPN is a hub-and-spoke VPN with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels, built from mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec. It scales without configuring a full mesh.
questions.discriminator_tested: DMVPN = mGRE, NHRP, IPsec.

questions.stem: What BEST describes what the configuration below creates?
questions.exhibit:
interface Tunnel10
 ip address 172.31.0.1 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source g0/0
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
 tunnel mode ipsec ipv4
 tunnel protection ipsec profile SITE-B

options.text: An encrypted tunnel to 203.0.113.2
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say what kind of tunnel.

options.text: A GRE tunnel protected by IPsec
options.rationale: GRE over IPsec would use 'tunnel mode gre'.

options.text: A route-based IPsec VTI, with no GRE header
options.rationale: Correct: 'tunnel mode ipsec ipv4' makes a VTI.

options.text: A DMVPN spoke with dynamic tunnels
options.rationale: DMVPN uses mGRE and NHRP.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI is an IPsec tunnel presented as a routable virtual interface: route-based, with no GRE header. Crypto maps are policy-based.
questions.discriminator_tested: VTI: route-based, no GRE header.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes PKI?

options.text: A symmetric key shared among users
options.rationale: PKI is built on public/private key pairs.

options.text: A single certificate used for a website
options.rationale: A certificate is one product of PKI.

options.text: The whole key trust system
options.rationale: Correct: CAs, certificates, policies, and processes together.

options.text: A server that issues certificates
options.rationale: That is a CA, one component.

questions.explanation: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the framework of CAs, certificates, policies, and processes that bind public keys to identities. It is the whole trust system, not one component.
questions.discriminator_tested: PKI is the whole trust system.

questions.stem: A browser shows the certificate path below. What BEST explains why it trusts portal.example.com's certificate?
questions.exhibit:
Certificate path
  Example Root CA          (in the trusted root store)
    Example Issuing CA
      portal.example.com

options.text: It was issued by Example Issuing CA
options.rationale: True, but that CA is trusted only because the root signed it.

options.text: Certificates on HTTPS sites are trusted automatically
options.rationale: Untrusted chains trigger warnings.

options.text: The website sent its private key for checking
options.rationale: Private keys are never sent.

options.text: It chains to a root CA the browser already trusts
options.rationale: Correct: each certificate is signed by the one above it, up to a trusted root.

questions.explanation: Certificate authorities are trusted entities that issue, sign, and revoke certificates. The root CA is the trust anchor, signing with its own private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: The CA is the trust anchor.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a certificate template from a certificate?

options.text: Templates are stored on the CA
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't explain the difference.

options.text: It's the blueprint; certificates are issued from it
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: They are the same document in different formats
options.rationale: A template is settings; a certificate is a signed document.

options.text: A template holds a private key; a certificate doesn't
options.rationale: Templates hold settings, not keys.

questions.explanation: A certificate template holds the predefined settings (key usage, validity, key size, subject fields) a CA applies when issuing certificates. It is the blueprint for issuance, not a certificate itself.
questions.discriminator_tested: Template = blueprint for issuance.

questions.stem: Which two checks does a client make when validating a server's certificate? (Choose two.)

options.text: That the current date is within its validity
options.rationale: Correct: expired or not-yet-valid certificates fail.

options.text: That the server's password is correct
options.rationale: Certificates don't involve passwords.

options.text: That the certificate is under 1 KB
options.rationale: Size isn't a validation check.

options.text: That a trusted CA's signature is valid
options.rationale: Correct: the signature proves who issued it.

options.text: That the certificate includes the private key
options.rationale: Certificates never contain the private key.

questions.explanation: Certificates are signed X.509 documents binding a public key to an identity. They are validated by the CA's signature, the validity dates, and revocation status, and they never hold the private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: Validated by CA signature, dates, and revocation status.

questions.stem: The entry 'access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0' was meant to permit the 192.168.1.0/24 network. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: ACL 10 is reserved for extended ACLs
options.rationale: 1-99 are standard numbers.

options.text: A standard ACL needs the 'tcp' keyword
options.rationale: Standard ACLs take no protocol.

options.text: Subnet mask used, not wildcard
options.rationale: Correct: the wildcard should be 0.0.0.255.

options.text: It won't match the intended hosts
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

questions.explanation: Standard ACL commands take a number, an action, and a source plus wildcard. A subnet mask used in place of a wildcard matches the wrong bits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACL: number, action, source plus wildcard.

questions.stem: Which traffic does the entry 'access-list 110 permit tcp host 10.1.4.20 10.1.9.0 0.0.0.255 eq 22' permit?

options.text: Any traffic from 10.1.4.20 to 10.1.9.0/24
options.rationale: The port limits it to TCP 22.
Correct: source host, destination subnet, TCP 22.
Source comes before destination; this is reversed.
Telnet is TCP 23.

questions.explanation: Extended ACL commands follow the order action, protocol, source, destination, then port.
questions.discriminator_tested: Order: action, protocol, source, destination, port.

questions.stem: Which command sequence creates a named extended ACL that permits HTTPS from anywhere?

options.text: ip access-list extended WEB-IN, then access-list permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Named ACL entries omit 'access-list'.

options.text: ip access-list WEB-IN, then permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: The 'extended' keyword is required.

options.text: access-list WEB-IN permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Names are used with 'ip access-list', not this syntax.

options.text: ip access-list extended WEB-IN, then permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Correct: the type keyword, then entries without 'access-list'.

questions.explanation: Named ACLs start with 'ip access-list extended NAME' (or 'standard'), then take entries such as 'permit tcp any any eq 443' in ACL config mode. Entries omit the 'access-list' keyword.
questions.discriminator_tested: Named ACLs need the type keyword; entries omit 'access-list'.

questions.stem: ACL 110 must filter traffic arriving at the router from the user LAN on interface g0/1. Which command applies it correctly?

options.text: ip access-group 110 out, under interface g0/1
options.rationale: 'out' filters traffic leaving toward the users.

options.text: ip access-group 110 in, under interface g0/1
options.rationale: Correct: 'in' is traffic entering the router on g0/1.

options.text: access-class 110 in, under line vty 0 4
options.rationale: That limits management sessions, not traffic.

options.text: ip access-group 110 in, in global config
options.rationale: access-group is an interface command.

questions.explanation: An ACL is applied with 'interface g0/1' then 'ip access-group 110 in' (or out). Direction is relative to the router, there is one ACL per protocol, interface, and direction, and an unapplied ACL filters nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Direction is relative to the router.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes 'access-class' from 'ip access-group'?

options.text: access-class filters traffic passing through
options.rationale: That is ip access-group.

options.text: It limits sessions to the device
options.rationale: Correct: it controls who can log in to the router itself.

options.text: access-class requires a named ACL
options.rationale: Numbered ACLs work too.

options.text: access-class is applied under line configuration
options.rationale: True, but where it is typed isn't what it does.

questions.explanation: Applying an ACL to VTY lines uses 'access-class 10 in'. access-class limits management sessions to the device; ip access-group filters traffic through an interface.
questions.discriminator_tested: access-class = sessions to the device; access-group = traffic through.

questions.stem: An engineer adds 'access-list 110 deny tcp any any eq 23' to numbered ACL 110, which ends with 'permit ip any any'. Telnet still works. What BEST explains why?

options.text: Numbered ACLs ignore entries added later
options.rationale: They accept them, at the end.

options.text: Telnet uses UDP 23, so it doesn't match
options.rationale: Telnet is TCP 23.

options.text: The permit matches Telnet first
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why the deny sits below it.

options.text: The new entry was appended after the permit-all
options.rationale: Correct: new numbered entries go to the end, below the broad permit.

questions.explanation: New numbered entries append to the end; sequence numbers allow inserting entries. A broad entry above a specific one shadows it.
questions.discriminator_tested: New entries append to the end; a broad entry shadows a later specific one.

questions.stem: Which entry body matches both SSH and Telnet in one line?

options.text: tcp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: Correct: 'range' with tcp covers both ports.

options.text: ip any any range 22 23
options.rationale: 'ip' can't take ports.

options.text: udp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: SSH and Telnet use TCP.

options.text: tcp any any gt 23
options.rationale: Matches ports above 23, missing both.

questions.explanation: Port and protocol keywords: protocols tcp, udp, icmp, ip; operators eq, neq, gt, lt, range. Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' can't take ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require tcp or udp; range for spans.

questions.stem: Interface g0/1 connects to the server LAN where 10.1.9.10 lives. Users' Telnet sessions to 10.1.9.10 still succeed, and the output below shows entry 10 with 0 matches. What is the MOST likely explanation?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show access-lists 110
Extended IP access list 110
    10 deny tcp any host 10.1.9.10 eq 23 (0 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (15233 matches)
R1# show ip interface g0/1 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is 110

options.text: Entry 10 isn't matching any packets
options.rationale: True, but that's the symptom, not the cause.

options.text: The ACL isn't applied to any interface
options.rationale: The output shows it applied inbound on g0/1.

options.text: The permit entry overrides the deny
options.rationale: The deny is first; order isn't the problem.

options.text: It's applied in the wrong direction
options.rationale: Correct: requests to the server leave g0/1 outbound; inbound sees only replies.

questions.explanation: When verifying ACLs, 'show access-lists' shows what the ACL says and its hits, and 'show ip interface' shows where it is applied. Zero hits on a deny that should match points to placement or direction.
questions.discriminator_tested: show access-lists = contents and hits; show ip interface = where applied.

questions.stem: Which command adds a note to ACL 110 explaining why an entry exists?

options.text: access-list 110 remark Block Telnet
options.rationale: Correct: 'remark' documents the ACL in the configuration.

options.text: no access-list 110
options.rationale: That deletes the whole ACL.

options.text: ! Block Telnet
options.rationale: A '!' comment isn't saved in the configuration.

options.text: access-list 110 description Block Telnet
options.rationale: 'description' is an interface command.

questions.explanation: 'remark' documents an entry. 'no ip access-group 110 in' removes only the application, while 'no access-list 110' deletes the whole ACL.
questions.discriminator_tested: remark documents; removing the application vs deleting the ACL.

questions.stem: To let OSPF run across an encrypted site-to-site link, an engineer configures a Cisco IPsec VTI instead of a policy-based crypto map. Which benefit of the VTI BEST explains why it suits this goal?

options.text: The tunnel is a routable interface that routing can run over
options.rationale: A VTI is route-based: the IPsec tunnel is a virtual interface, so OSPF and other protocols treat it like any link.

options.text: The tunnel omits the GRE header that GRE-over-IPsec adds
options.rationale: A VTI does avoid the GRE header, a real advantage, but that is not what lets the routing protocol run; the routable interface is.

options.text: AH in transport mode authenticates each packet end to end
options.rationale: AH provides authentication without encryption and does not create a routable tunnel interface.

options.text: An extended ACL selects exactly which traffic gets encrypted
options.rationale: Selecting encrypted traffic with an ACL describes the policy-based crypto-map approach the VTI replaces.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI is route-based, presenting the tunnel as a virtual interface so dynamic routing protocols can run directly over the encrypted path, unlike policy-based crypto maps. It also drops the GRE header, but the routable interface is what enables routing here.
questions.discriminator_tested: An IPsec VTI is a route-based, GRE-free virtual interface you can route over, unlike policy-based crypto maps or non-encrypting AH.

questions.stem: A browser shows the certificate chain below for portal.example.com. What BEST explains why the browser trusts it?
questions.exhibit:
Certificate chain for portal.example.com
  [0] Subject: CN=portal.example.com
      Issuer:  CN=Example Issuing CA
  [1] Subject: CN=Example Issuing CA
      Issuer:  CN=Example Root CA
  [2] Subject: CN=Example Root CA
      Issuer:  CN=Example Root CA  (self-signed)
Trusted roots on this device: Example Root CA

options.text: The certificate's own public key proves the site's identity directly
options.rationale: A certificate's public key alone proves nothing without a trusted CA's signature vouching for it.

options.text: Example Issuing CA issued the certificate for portal.example.com
options.rationale: The issuing CA did sign this certificate, but it is trusted only because the trusted root signed it in turn.

options.text: A root CA already in the device's trust store signed the chain
options.rationale: Trust flows from a root the device already trusts; its signature validates the intermediate, which validates the server certificate.

options.text: The certificate is self-signed and validates on its own
options.rationale: This certificate is not self-signed; it chains through an intermediate up to a trusted root.

questions.explanation: A CA is the trust anchor because a root the device already trusts signs the chain with its private key, and that signature is what makes the leaf certificate trustworthy. Being issued by some CA is not enough unless that CA chains to a trusted root.
questions.discriminator_tested: A certificate is trusted because a root CA in the trust store signed its chain, not merely because some CA issued it.

questions.stem: A router shows the output below. Which statement BEST describes this configuration?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show access-lists
Extended IP access list WEB-IN
    10 permit tcp any host 198.51.100.10 eq 443
    20 permit tcp any host 198.51.100.10 eq 80
    30 deny ip any any

options.text: An ACL whose entries each need the 'access-list' keyword
options.rationale: Entries in a named ACL are entered without the access-list keyword, as the numbered lines show.

options.text: A standard ACL that matches on source address
options.rationale: A standard ACL can match source addresses; this one matches destinations and ports, so it is extended.

options.text: An extended named ACL filtering by destination and port
options.rationale: The Extended header and the destination-host, port matches show it is an extended named ACL; the standard or extended keyword is required when creating one.

options.text: An ACL that allows web traffic to one internal server
options.rationale: It does allow web traffic to that server, but this omits that it is extended and ends with an explicit deny.

questions.explanation: A named ACL is created with ip access-list followed by standard or extended, and its entries are typed inside ACL config mode without the access-list keyword. The Extended header and destination/port matching identify this one as extended.
questions.discriminator_tested: Named ACLs require the standard or extended keyword at creation, and their entries omit the access-list keyword used by numbered ACLs.

questions.stem: An administrator wants a single ACL entry that matches both SSH and Telnet to any destination. Which entry body BEST matches both in one line?

options.text: ip any any range 22 23
options.rationale: The ip keyword matches all IP traffic and cannot take port numbers, so this entry is rejected.

options.text: udp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: The syntax is valid, but SSH and Telnet run over TCP, so matching UDP ports 22-23 catches the wrong traffic.

options.text: tcp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: A port range needs a transport protocol; tcp with range 22 23 matches TCP ports 22 and 23 in one entry, covering SSH and Telnet.

options.text: tcp any any eq 22
options.rationale: This is valid, but eq 22 matches only SSH, so it does not include Telnet.

questions.explanation: Port numbers require a transport protocol keyword such as tcp or udp, and the range operator takes two ports; ip matches every protocol and cannot specify ports. Since SSH and Telnet are TCP, tcp ... range 22 23 is the correct single entry.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require tcp or udp and a port operator; the ip keyword matches all traffic and cannot take port numbers.

questions.stem: An engineer replaces a policy-based crypto map with a route-based IPsec VTI so OSPF can run over the tunnel. Because a VTI is a routable interface, what is the MAIN consequence the engineer must plan for?

options.text: An extended ACL must still spell out exactly which traffic to encrypt first
options.rationale: Selecting encrypted traffic with an ACL is the policy-based crypto-map method the VTI replaces, not something still required.

options.text: It removes the GRE header that GRE-over-IPsec would add
options.rationale: Dropping the GRE header is a real VTI advantage, but it is a benefit, not the operational consequence to manage.

options.text: AH will authenticate but not encrypt the tunneled packets
options.rationale: AH authenticates without encrypting and does not create a routable tunnel, so it is unrelated to this design.

options.text: Routing, not an ACL, now decides which traffic the tunnel protects
options.rationale: A VTI is route-based, so whatever routing sends into the interface is encrypted; a routing mistake can misdirect or expose traffic.

questions.explanation: Because a VTI presents IPsec as a routable interface, routing (not an ACL) determines what is protected, so routing errors become a security and availability concern. Dropping the GRE header is a benefit of the VTI, and ACL-based selection describes the crypto-map approach it replaces.
questions.discriminator_tested: A route-based VTI protects whatever routing sends into it, shifting traffic selection from an ACL to the routing table.

questions.stem: A team stands up the components summarized below. Which two statements BEST describe what has been built? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
InternalTrust deployment summary
  Root CA:            corp-root-ca (offline)
  Issuing CA:         corp-issuing-ca
  Certificate templates: Workstation, WebServer, User
  Policies:           issuance + revocation (CRL every 24h)
  Enrollment:         auto-enroll for domain laptops

options.text: A public key infrastructure (PKI), the full trust system
options.rationale: CAs, templates, issuance and revocation policies, and enrollment together form a PKI, the overall certificate-trust system.

options.text: A symmetric-key system where parties share one secret key
options.rationale: Symmetric-key systems share one secret and are unrelated to certificate-based public-key trust.

options.text: A single server certificate issued for one public website
options.rationale: A lone server certificate is a single artifact a PKI can issue, not the whole infrastructure described.

options.text: A certificate authority, which is just one part of this build
options.rationale: A CA is only one component of what was built; the deployment also includes templates, policies, and enrollment.

options.text: A framework binding public keys to identities via CAs
options.rationale: PKI is precisely a framework that binds public keys to identities using CAs and policies, which the summary lists.

questions.explanation: A PKI is the entire framework of CAs, certificates, templates, policies, and enrollment that binds public keys to identities. Naming only the certificate authority captures a single component, not the system as a whole.
questions.discriminator_tested: PKI is the complete certificate trust framework; a CA is just one part within it.

questions.stem: A browser trusts portal.example.com. The site's certificate was issued by 'Example Issuing CA', which in turn chains up to 'Example Root CA', and that root is the one in the browser's trust store. What BEST explains the trust?

options.text: A root CA already trusted by the browser signed the chain
options.rationale: Trust flows from a root the browser already holds; its signature validates the issuing CA, which validates the site certificate.

options.text: The certificate is self-signed and needs no issuer
options.rationale: This certificate is not self-signed; it chains through an issuing CA up to the trusted root.

options.text: The certificate's own public key vouches for the site
options.rationale: A certificate's public key alone proves nothing without a trusted CA's signature over it.

options.text: The issuing CA that signed the certificate is named in it
options.rationale: The issuing CA did sign the certificate, but that matters only because the trusted root vouches for that issuing CA.

questions.explanation: A certificate is trusted because a CA already in the trust store signed the chain with its private key, anchoring the issuing CA and then the site certificate. Being issued by some CA is not enough unless that CA chains to a trusted root.
questions.discriminator_tested: Trust comes from a root CA in the trust store signing the chain, not merely from the certificate having an issuer.

questions.stem: The configuration below creates a named ACL. Which two statements about this syntax are correct? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended WEB-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp any host 198.51.100.10 eq 443
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any

options.text: The same rule could be written as a numbered standard ACL
options.rationale: This rule matches on destination and port, which a standard ACL cannot express, so it is not interchangeable.

options.text: Each permit or deny line must start with `access-list`
options.rationale: Beginning each line with `access-list` is numbered-ACL syntax; named ACL entries do not, so this is the common mistake.

options.text: Naming the ACL requires the `standard` or `extended` keyword
options.rationale: A named ACL must be created with `ip access-list` followed by `standard` or `extended`; the keyword is mandatory.

options.text: A named ACL's name must be a number from 100 to 199
options.rationale: A named ACL uses a name, not a 100-199 number; that range belongs to numbered extended ACLs.

options.text: Its entries omit the `access-list` keyword
options.rationale: Inside ACL config mode the permit/deny entries are entered without the `access-list` keyword numbered ACLs use.

questions.explanation: Named ACLs require `standard` or `extended` at creation and then take entries without the `access-list` keyword. Beginning each entry with `access-list` is the numbered-ACL syntax and is the frequent error.
questions.discriminator_tested: Named ACLs need the standard/extended keyword and drop the `access-list` prefix on their entries.

questions.stem: An administrator tries to permit both SSH and Telnet in one ACL entry and types `permit ip any any range 22 23`, but the router rejects it. Which two facts explain the failure? (Choose two.)

options.text: SSH and Telnet use UDP, so `udp` is required here
options.rationale: SSH and Telnet run over TCP, not UDP, so `udp` would match the wrong traffic.

options.text: The `ip` keyword matches all protocols and cannot specify ports
options.rationale: `ip` matches every protocol and has no concept of ports, so appending a port range is invalid.

options.text: Port numbers like 22 and 23 require `tcp` or `udp` instead
options.rationale: Port numbers need a transport protocol keyword; `tcp` must replace `ip` to use ports 22 and 23.

options.text: `range 22 23` is invalid because ranges need three ports
options.rationale: A `range` takes two ports, not three; the range itself is fine once the protocol is `tcp`.

options.text: The entry must use `eq` since `range` is not a valid operator
options.rationale: `range` is a valid operator; the problem is `ip` cannot take ports, not the operator.

questions.explanation: Port numbers are only valid with a transport protocol such as `tcp` or `udp`; the `ip` keyword matches all protocols and cannot specify ports. Using `permit tcp any any range 22 23` would correctly match SSH and Telnet.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require `tcp`/`udp`; the `ip` keyword matches all traffic and rejects port operands.

questions.stem: An engineer replaces a policy-based crypto map between two sites with a Cisco IPsec static VTI (tunnel mode ipsec ipv4) and then configures dynamic routing between the sites. Which two effects BEST describe the result of this change? (Choose two.)

options.text: Traffic is still protected by ESP, as it was before
options.rationale: ESP does still provide encryption, but that isn't an effect of the change; both designs use IPsec ESP.

options.text: Packets drop a GRE header that the crypto map used to add
options.rationale: Crypto maps don't add a GRE header; GRE appears in GRE-over-IPsec designs, which a VTI makes unnecessary.

options.text: Branch sites now build direct tunnels to each other on demand
options.rationale: On-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels describe Cisco DMVPN, not a point-to-point static VTI.

options.text: OSPF hellos now cross the link, so neighbors can form
options.rationale: Correct: a VTI is a routable virtual interface that carries multicast, so routing-protocol hellos pass and adjacencies form; a crypto map offers no interface to peer over.

options.text: Routes toward the tunnel decide what traffic is encrypted
options.rationale: Correct: with a route-based VTI, whatever is routed into the tunnel interface is encrypted, replacing the crypto ACL that a policy-based crypto map uses to select traffic.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI makes the tunnel a routable interface: routing protocols run over it and the routing table decides what is encrypted. A policy-based crypto map instead selects traffic with a crypto ACL and has no interface, which is why designs that needed routing used to add GRE over IPsec.
questions.discriminator_tested: VTIs are route-based and steer traffic into encryption through routing, whereas crypto maps are policy-based and match traffic with an ACL.

questions.stem: An analyst inspects the certificate shown in the exhibit on a company laptop. What BEST classifies this certificate?
questions.exhibit:
Subject:            CN=Example Root CA, O=Example Corp
Issuer:             CN=Example Root CA, O=Example Corp
Basic Constraints:  CA:TRUE
Key Usage:          Certificate Sign, CRL Sign
Store:              Trusted Root Certification Authorities
Has signed:         CN=Example Issuing CA, O=Example Corp

options.text: A certificate template defining issuance settings
options.rationale: A certificate template is a configuration on the CA that sets options for issued certificates; it isn't a certificate in the trust store.

options.text: A self-signed server certificate the browser should reject
options.rationale: Self-signed doesn't mean untrusted: roots are self-signed by design, and this one is a CA in the trusted root store, not a server certificate.

options.text: A root CA certificate acting as the trust anchor
options.rationale: Correct: subject and issuer match, it is a CA that signs other CA certificates, and it sits in the trusted root store, so it is the trust anchor whose private key signs the chain.

options.text: An intermediate CA certificate that issues to users
options.rationale: It is a CA certificate, but an intermediate is issued by a different CA; here the subject and issuer are the same, which marks the root.

questions.explanation: A certificate authority is trusted because it signs certificates with its own private key, and the root CA is self-signed and stored as the trust anchor. Intermediate CAs are trusted only because the root signed them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Matching subject and issuer plus placement in the trusted store identify the root CA, the anchor that every chain leads back to.

questions.stem: An administrator pastes the configuration in the exhibit into a router during a change window. The router reports errors on the first three lines but accepts the interface commands, and the administrator closes the ticket without verifying. What is the MOST likely consequence?
questions.exhibit:
ip access-list WEB-IN
 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 443
 deny ip any any log
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip access-group WEB-IN in

options.text: Inbound traffic passes unfiltered; no WEB-IN ACL exists
options.rationale: Correct: without the standard or extended keyword the ACL isn't created, its entries are rejected too, and an access-group that references an undefined ACL filters nothing.

options.text: The HTTPS server stays reachable as the change intended
options.rationale: HTTPS does stay reachable, but so does every other inbound flow, which is the real exposure.

options.text: HTTPS alone reaches the server, as the entries intended
options.rationale: This assumes the ACL was built, but the missing extended keyword made the router reject it and its entries.

options.text: Traffic is dropped by the implicit deny at the ACL's end
options.rationale: The implicit deny applies to an ACL that has entries; an access-group pointing at an ACL that doesn't exist lets traffic through instead.

questions.explanation: A named ACL must be created with 'ip access-list standard' or 'ip access-list extended' followed by the name, and its entries are then typed without the 'access-list' keyword. Leaving out the type keyword means the ACL is never created, so the interface ends up with no filtering.
questions.discriminator_tested: Creating a named ACL requires the standard or extended type keyword before the name; without it, no list is built.
